content.text: CORS is a browser mechanism for relaxing the same-origin policy: it tells browsers which other origins may read your responses. Your server still runs every request, and curl, scripts and other servers ignore CORS entirely. Protect the API with authentication and authorization, and keep CORS an exact list of the origins that need it, especially when credentials are allowed.

A partner review turns up a surprise: the reviewer downloads the internal price list with one curl command. The endpoint has no login, because the team considered it protected: the CORS policy only allows
https://shop.example

. To prove it, a developer calls the same endpoint from a page on another domain, and the browser console prints "blocked by CORS policy". Both results are real. Neither one means what the team thought.
The common misconception
The belief: CORS is a server-side firewall for origins. List the allowed origins, and requests from everyone else are rejected, so the API only answers your own front end.
The evidence looks convincing. Call the API from another site and the console says the request was blocked. The policy sits in
Program.cs
next to authentication, behind a method named
WithOrigins

, and many tutorials describe it as restricting who can access your API. CORS errors are also a daily annoyance during development, which makes CORS feel like a strict gatekeeper. But that block happens in the browser, after your server has already answered.
What actually happens
The server answers, the browser decides who reads

Microsoft's CORS docs say it directly: "It's up to the client (browser) to enforce CORS. The server executes the request and returns the response, it's the client that returns an error and blocks the response." We checked with a small ASP.NET Core 10 app whose policy allows only
https://shop.example
, called four ways:

blocks.code:
Client                              Status  CORS allow header     Body
curl, no Origin                     200     none                  read
curl, Origin: https://evil.example  200     none                  read
curl, Origin: https://shop.example  200     https://shop.example  read
Chromium 156, page on other origin  200     none                  blocked

content.text: The server log shows the handler ran and returned 200 all four times. Only the browser refused to hand the body to the page, with
TypeError: Failed to fetch
and the console message "No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource."
CORS loosens the same-origin policy, it doesn't add a wall
The
same-origin policy

is the real browser rule, and MDN describes its shape: "Cross-origin writes are typically allowed. Examples are links, redirects, and form submissions." while "Cross-origin reads are typically disallowed".
CORS
is the opt-in that lets you make exceptions for reads. That's why Microsoft lists it as something that "Is not a security feature, CORS relaxes security. An API is not safer by allowing CORS."
Some requests are checked first. For methods and headers a plain form can't produce, the browser sends a
preflight
OPTIONS

request and waits for approval. But a request that looks like a form submission goes out without asking. MDN notes the server "still must opt-in using Access-Control-Allow-Origin to share the response with the script", which controls reading, not whether the request arrives.
Origin is a browser claim, not a client identity
Inside a browser, the Fetch Standard makes
Origin
a forbidden header "so the user agent remains in full control" over it, which is why it helps against CSRF. Outside a browser it's an ordinary header: our curl claimed to be
https://shop.example
and got the allow header back. CORS can't tell your front end from a script, and it was never meant to. The Fetch Standard says that sending
Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *
on a public resource shares it with browser APIs "much like it is already shared with curl and wget."
What CORS does protect: data reached through your users

The Fetch Standard explains why CORS had to be opt-in: "to prevent leaking data from responses behind a firewall (intranets). Additionally, for requests including credentials it needs to be opt-in to prevent leaking potentially-sensitive data." So the real risk is the opposite of the myth: a policy that's too open. Reflect any origin and allow credentials, and any site a signed-in user visits can read their data with their cookies. The standard calls that combination "rather unsafe", and the OWASP Top 10 2025 lists "CORS misconfiguration allows API access from unauthorized or untrusted origins" under A01 Broken Access Control.
Put access control in the API

tabs.label: ❌ Wrong
✅ Right

content.text: The fixed version splits the two jobs.
RequireAuthorization

decides who may call an endpoint, and it runs for every client. CORS only decides which web pages may read the answer in a browser, so it lists the one origin that needs it. Microsoft names the trap in the wrong version: "Bypassing the built-in checks by using
SetIsOriginAllowed(_ => true)
together with
AllowCredentials
is also an insecure configuration."

rows.text: May a script on another site read this response?
May curl, Postman or a server call this endpoint?
Does the handler run for a disallowed origin?
Can another site make a user's browser send a form POST?
May this caller see this particular record?

content.text: A policy that copies any
Origin
into
Access-Control-Allow-Origin
and also allows credentials lets every website read your users' data through their own browsers, with their own cookies. That's the configuration this mechanism exists to prevent.
If
curl

with no credentials gets data back, the endpoint is public, whatever the CORS policy says. And when a CORS error shows up during development, add the exact origin for that environment instead of widening the policy.
CORS works on origins: scheme, host and port must all match.
https://app.example.com
and
https://api.example.com
are different origins, so they need CORS between them, even though they're the same site for cookies.
How to apply it in your project

items.title: Assume every client can call every endpoint

content.text: Put authentication and authorization on each endpoint that isn't meant to be public. CORS doesn't change that list.

items.title: Make the policy an exact list

content.text: Name each allowed origin. No reflection, no
with credentials, and wildcard subdomains only if you trust every subdomain.

items.title: Allow credentials only when the front end needs them

content.text: If your front end calls the API with a bearer token, it doesn't need
AllowCredentials
, and leaving it off removes the cookie risk.
Keep a separate list per environment, so
localhost
never ships to production and nobody widens the policy to fix a dev error.
Call each protected endpoint with curl and no credentials, and from a page on a non-allowed origin. Both should fail, for different reasons.
Key takeaways

items.text: CORS controls which web pages may read your responses in a browser, not who may call your API.
The server runs the request either way; the browser only withholds the response from the page.
Non-browser clients ignore CORS and can send any
Real access control is authentication and authorization, enforced on the server for every request.
An open CORS policy with credentials is the dangerous case; keep the allowed origins exact.
